title: Conjugation, aromaticity and EAS
note: A ring is aromatic if it is cyclic, planar, fully conjugated, and holds 4n + 2 π electrons (2, 6, 10...). In electrophilic aromatic substitution, an electrophile adds to give a resonance-stabilized arenium ion, then loss of H⁺ restores the aromatic ring. Activators direct ortho/para; most deactivators direct meta, but halogens deactivate and still direct ortho/para.

read.title: Why benzene resists addition
text: Benzene has three C=C bonds on paper, yet it does not add bromine the way an alkene does. Its six π electrons are delocalized over a flat ring, giving extra stability called aromaticity. Hückel's rule states the requirement: a planar, cyclic, fully conjugated system with 4n + 2 π electrons. Six (n = 1) fits, which is why the cyclopentadienyl anion and the tropylium cation are aromatic, while planar cyclobutadiene, with four, is antiaromatic.

Because addition would destroy aromaticity, benzene undergoes substitution instead. A strong electrophile, such as Br⁺ generated with FeBr₃ or NO₂⁺ from nitric and sulfuric acids, accepts a pair of π electrons. This forms an arenium ion, a carbocation spread over three ring carbons. A base then removes the proton from the carbon bearing the electrophile, and the aromatic ring returns.

Groups already on the ring control both rate and position. Donors such as –OH and –NH₂ push electron density into the ring, speeding the reaction and stabilizing attack at the ortho and para positions. Withdrawing groups such as –NO₂ slow the reaction, and attack at the meta position avoids placing positive charge next to them. Halogens are the exception: they withdraw inductively but donate a lone pair by resonance, so they deactivate yet direct ortho/para.

q.q: Why does benzene undergo substitution rather than addition?
